title: At the Market
grammarNote: This lesson covers demonstratives (este/esta/estos/ese/aquel) agreeing in gender and number with the noun they modify, plus querer and poder used as everyday request verbs when shopping. It also introduces quantities (un kilo, medio kilo, una docena) and the singular/plural contrast between ¿cuánto cuesta? and ¿cuánto cuestan?.

phrases.native: How much does this mango cost?
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Este' is the masculine singular demonstrative ('this'), used for something close to the speaker; it agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
phrases.grammarNote: 'Cuesta' is the singular form of costar, used because 'mango' is singular; the demonstrative 'este' must match masculine singular nouns like 'mango'.
phrases.memoryHook: Picture pointing at 'this' mango right ESTE (here) at your feet — este = 'this here'.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: How much does this mango cost?
Estás en el mercado y quieres saber el precio de un mango. ¿Qué preguntas?

phrases.native: How much do these tomatoes cost?
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Cuestan' is the plural form of costar, and 'estos' is the masculine plural demonstrative — both must agree with the plural noun 'tomates'.

exampleSentence.target: Estos tomates cuestan quince pesos el kilo.
exampleSentence.native: These tomatoes cost fifteen pesos a kilo.

phrases.grammarNote: Use 'cuesta' with singular nouns and 'cuestan' with plural nouns; 'estos' (not 'este') matches the plural noun 'tomates'.
phrases.memoryHook: Add an 'n' for más de uno — cuestan has an 'n' like 'niños' (kids, plural).

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: How much do these tomatoes cost?
Ves varios tomates juntos en el puesto y quieres saber el precio de todos. ¿Qué preguntas?

phrases.native: I want a kilo of mangoes
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Quiero' (from querer) is the most direct way to state what you want when shopping; 'un kilo de' + noun is the standard way to order produce by weight.

exampleSentence.target: Quiero un kilo de mangos, por favor.
exampleSentence.native: I want a kilo of mangoes, please.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Querer' is an irregular e→ie stem-changing verb: quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren.
phrases.memoryHook: Quiero sounds like 'key-AIR-oh' — the 'key' unlocks what you want.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: I want a kilo of mangoes
___ un kilo de mangos, por favor.
Estás en el puesto de frutas y quieres un kilo de mangos. ¿Qué le dices al marchante?

phrases.native: Can you give me half a kilo?
phrases.vocabularyIntro: '¿Me puede dar...?' uses poder (can/to be able) plus the indirect object 'me' to make a polite request; 'medio kilo' means half a kilo.

exampleSentence.target: ¿Me puede dar medio kilo de tomates?
exampleSentence.native: Can you give me half a kilo of tomatoes?

phrases.grammarNote: 'Puede' is the usted form of poder (o→ue stem-changing verb), keeping the request formal and polite when addressing a vendor.
phrases.memoryHook: Medio kilo = half of a full kilo, like cutting a KEE-loh in half with a MEH (halfway mark).

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: Can you give me half a kilo?
Solo necesitas la mitad de un kilo de fruta. ¿Qué le pides al marchante?

phrases.target: Esa fruta se ve muy fresca
phrases.phonetic: EH-sah FROO-tah seh veh mwee FRES-kah

phrases.native: Those plantains over there are cheap
Can you give me a little more?
phrases.phonetic: meh PWEH-deh dar oon POH-koh mahs

phrases.native: Could you give me the change, please?
phrases.phonetic: meh dah el KAHM-bee-oh, por fah-VOR

dialogue.scenario: You buy mangos and tomatoes from a vendor at a Mexican market, negotiate the quantity, and pay.
